name: lsblk
summary: Disks and partitions as a tree

examples.does: Disks, partitions and LVM volumes, with sizes and mount points
Add filesystem type, label and UUID
Chosen columns

pitfalls: A new, empty disk shows as TYPE disk with no partitions below it and no mount point.

name: blkid
summary: Filesystem type, label and UUID of partitions

examples.does: Every partition with its type, label and UUID
Only the UUID, ready for /etc/fstab

pitfalls: Use UUIDs in /etc/fstab, not /dev/sdX names: those can change between boots.

name: mount
summary: Attach a filesystem to a folder

examples.does: Mount a partition on /mnt until reboot
Mount everything in /etc/fstab: test fstab changes before rebooting
Make the root filesystem writable again (e.g. in recovery)

pitfalls: A wrong /etc/fstab line can stop the server booting. Run sudo mount -a and findmnt --verify after every edit.

name: umount

examples.does: Unmount
Detach now, finish when no longer used (lazy)

pitfalls: 'target is busy': find who uses it with sudo lsof +D /mnt or sudo fuser -vm /mnt. cd out of it yourself too.

examples.does: Every mount as a tree
Which mount a path is on
Check /etc/fstab for mistakes
Only these filesystem types

name: fdisk

examples.does: Every disk and its partitions
Edit partitions interactively; nothing is written until you press w

pitfalls: Check the disk name twice with lsblk. Writing to the wrong disk destroys its data.

name: parted

examples.does: Every disk and its partitions
One disk's partitions

examples.cmd: sudo parted -s /dev/<DISK> mklabel gpt mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%
examples.does: New GPT table with one partition filling the disk (erases the old table)

pitfalls: parted writes each change immediately; there is no 'write at the end' as in fdisk.

name: mkfs.ext4
summary: Create an ext4 filesystem (erases the partition)

examples.does: Create ext4 with a label

pitfalls: Everything on the partition is lost. Check the name with lsblk -f first.

name: mkfs.xfs
summary: Create an XFS filesystem (erases the partition)

examples.does: Create XFS with a label

pitfalls: XFS can grow but never shrink.

name: resize2fs
summary: Grow or shrink an ext4 filesystem
tasks: filesystem did not grow after extending the disk

examples.does: Grow ext4 to fill its (already enlarged) volume; works while mounted

pitfalls: To shrink: unmount, shrink the filesystem first, then the volume. The other order destroys data.

examples.does: Grow a mounted XFS filesystem to fill its volume (give the mount point)

name: e2fsck

examples.does: Check only, answer no to every repair
Full check and repair

pitfalls: Never repair a mounted filesystem: unmount it first (or boot into recovery for /).

name: pvs
summary: LVM physical volumes (disks given to LVM)

examples.does: Each LVM disk, its volume group, size and free space

name: vgs

examples.does: Each volume group with its size and free space (VFree)

pitfalls: Ubuntu's installer names the group ubuntu-vg by default, but check: it can differ.

examples.does: Each logical volume with its group and size
Add which disks each volume sits on

name: pvcreate

examples.does: Mark a disk as an LVM physical volume (overwrites what is on it)

pitfalls: Make sure the disk is the new, empty one: lsblk shows no partitions and no mount point.

name: vgextend
summary: Add a disk to a volume group
tasks: add a disk to a volume group

examples.does: Add the prepared disk's space to the group

name: lvextend
tasks: use all free space in the volume group

examples.does: Add 20 GB and grow the filesystem in the same step (-r)
Use all the group's free space

pitfalls: Without -r only the volume grows; df shows no change until you grow the filesystem (resize2fs or xfs_growfs).

name: lvcreate
summary: Create a logical volume or snapshot

examples.does: Create a 50 GB volume called data
A snapshot to roll back to; 5 GB holds the changes made after it

pitfalls: A snapshot that fills up becomes unusable. Make it big enough and remove it when done (lvremove).

name: mdadm

examples.does: State of one array and each of its disks
One line per array (the format of /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf)
Add a replacement disk; the array rebuilds onto it

pitfalls: After changing arrays, update /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf and run sudo update-initramfs -u.

examples.does: Swap files and partitions in use, with sizes
Turn on all swap listed in /etc/fstab

name: smartctl

examples.does: Overall health: PASSED or FAILED
Every attribute and the error log
Start a short self-test (a few minutes; read the result with -a)

pitfalls: smartctl is in the smartmontools package; install it if the command is missing.
Virtual machine disks usually have no SMART data.
